To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the color appearance of spots can be modeled as a Bayesian process in which the prior is the statistics of natural scenes and the posterior is the color name assigned by an observer to the spot, and that the model is consistent with the color naming data for spots, larger spots, and sinusoidal contrast modulating gratings.
the color naming of small spots is consistent with a model that incorporates the spatio-chromatically varying statistics of natural images and the individual variation of the cone mosaics.
the color appearance of a small spot is determined by the average chromatic signal of the spot reconstructed from the responses of the individual cones actually present in that spot.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how a complex visual system can be understood as an information processing device that operates in the presence of noise.
the problem of how color vision arises from the sampling of the visual world by the cone mosaic.
the problem of how the brain recovers information that has been lost during the sampling process.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed a new model of color vision that can account for the color naming data and that can be used to make testable predictions for experiments that probe how color appearance varies with the fine details of the retinal cone mosaic.

the model can explain the data of Hofer et al. (2005) in terms of the spatio-chromatic statistics of natural images, the optics and the topography of the individual observers' retinas, and the spatio-chrome distribution of the stimuli.
we have shown that the human visual system has the ability to reconstruct the color signals from the mosaic of cones, even when the mosaic has a very complex geometry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a Bayesian model that incorporates the optics and topography of individual retinas, as well as a plausible prior over natural scenes, can explain the data from a wide variety of experiments.
color appearance is not just a property of a small spot, it is also a property of the cone mosaic.
a Bayesian model can be constructed to predict the color appearance of spots of a size comparable to a single cone, and the predictions are consistent with the data.
